chunks: "I'd decide based on three things: can the motor be serviced, what shape is the rest of it in, and the economics. First, serviceability.
Larger motors, power tools, industrial and automotive motors are designed with accessible brush holders and standard brush sets, so replacing brushes is routine maintenance.
Small sealed motors, the can motors in toys, small gearmotors, or phone-size devices have brushes that are part of the can and not replaceable, so when the brushes wear out you replace the motor.
If the motor is serviceable, I look at the commutator: is it round, with an even brown film, no deep grooves, burnt bars or high mica, and still above its minimum diameter?
Then bearings: no play or noise. Windings: resistance balanced between segments, insulation resistance fine, no burnt smell. Magnets intact.
If all of that is good and only the brushes are worn, new brushes bring it back to like-new.
If the commutator is scored or burnt, I'd resurface it if the motor is valuable and there's material left; otherwise replace the motor.
If the windings or bearings are failing, I'd replace the motor. Third, economics: brush kit plus labour and downtime versus the cost of a new motor and its remaining life.
And I'd always ask why the brushes wore out: if it's overload or arcing, fix the cause or the new brushes will fail again."
